newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch publisher Wegener says media mix is right.
newsitem.headline: Dutch publisher Wegener says media mix is right.

text.p: Dutch publisher Wegener NV believes it has the right media mix to thrive in an increasingly crowded media market place.
Chairman Jan Houwert said in an interview that Wegener could reach the mass market through its regional newspapers while targeting individual consumers via direct marketing.
Furthermore, he said, the 1996 takeover of the Arcade music group had given Wegener a foothold in the entertainment business and a launchpad for further expansion outside the Netherlands.
Wegener, with annual sales of 1.5 billion guilders ($772.8 million), is the Netherlands' biggest regional newspaper publisher and its leading provider of direct marketing services.
"Newspaper publishing is mass communication and direct marketing is one-to-one communication, but new technology is bringing them closer together," Houwert said.
New technology has also enabled Wegener's direct marketing units to gather precise information about consumers and deliver individualised advertising and marketing packages to them.
"We are shooting with bullets these days instead of with buckshot," he said.

Houwert rejected the suggestion that Wegener's acquisition of Arcade had been mis-timed in view of the continuing weakness of the European market for compact discs. He said it was an important strategic move for the long term.

In addition to an extra source of revenue and potential synergy benefits, he said, it "gave us a presence in the rest of Europe which we can also use as a springboard for growth in other sectors like direct marketing, electronic publishing and cartography."

To tackle the malaise in the CD market, Wegener is shifting away from licensed multi-artist compilations, which have been hit by severe pressure on margins, and developing its own catalogue of original repertoire, Houwert said.
It has recently acquired music labels in France and Spain and plans further expansion of its own catalogue.
Houwert said Wegener had begun exploiting the potential synergies of the Arcade deal by using its print, radio and television media to market and publicise Arcade CDs.
The Music Factory (TMF), Wegener's music-video TV channel, is now watched by more young Dutch people than MTV Europe.

TMF, launched in 1995, should break even this year and start making a profit from 1998, Houwert said, while the group's Radio 10 Gold station, already profitable, would benefit from extra listeners after recently winning an FM frequency.
Houwert said that because Wegener was not active in a high-margin segment of the publishing industry, it was all the more important to run a tight ship.
A phased reduction in the number of the group's printing plants from nine to four is due to be completed this year.
"We're always looking for ways to improve unit production costs and I'm convinced that will continue," Houwert said.

Operating margins were not high, averaging about eight percent of revenues in recent years, but Houwert said a company like supermarkets group Ahold had shown that good money could still be made on even lower margins.
"What we aim for is profit growth, pure and simple, and growth of earnings per share," he said.
Wegener has posted an increase in earnings per share for each of the last 13 years and has forecast an increase this year of at least 10 percent.

Houwert saw the Internet becoming an important and commercially viable medium in the near future, allowing advertisers to communicate very selectively with consumers and measure exactly how many people they were reaching.
Wegener recently acquired Riverland Networks, a Dutch firm which designs and maintains websites and which will operate in future under the name of Netcast.

In collaboration with fellow publisher VNU, it has also launched City Online, a series of websites providing local news and information plus content from advertisers or links to the advertiser's own website.
Houwert said the project was still in its early days, but was already attracting interest from advertisers keen to experiment with the new medium.
